data.title: Gold's 37% slide from record looks overdone, says Saxo's Hansen, but $3,590 is the test
data.description:
Gold's moves are being set by the dollar and US rate pricing, not by safe-haven demand, so US data and Fed commentary will matter more than geopolitical headlines for any rebound. Because speculative positioning has been cut so hard, short covering could make any bounce sharp, especially in silver, the most stretched metal. A failure back below Wednesday's low would suggest forced selling has further to run. That would be a risk for miners and leveraged exposure. A softer dollar or a dovish shift in Fed expectations is the catalyst most likely to turn a technical rebound into a lasting one.

---

data.title: ECB picks Spain's Hernández de Cos as president, with 3 tests waiting from day one
data.description:
For bonds, the appointment matters most for the gap between French and German yields. Markets may treat a president who backed quantitative easing as a slightly firmer safety net for French debt, but his record on fiscal discipline makes a blanket rescue unlikely. That leaves French spreads tied to the election campaign more than to the ECB. The euro's immediate reaction is likely to be muted, since Hernández de Cos is seen as a continuity candidate, not someone who will change the direction of rates. Brunnermeier as chief economist is worth watching, as his academic work on financial stability could shape how the bank thinks about stepping into markets.

---

data.title: JPMorgan sees bitcoin capitulation in record Strategy discount, but 3 risks cloud the call
data.description:
For bitcoin, the June closing low near $58,500 is now the key level. A clean break would put the next on-chain support clusters, around $57,000 and then $47,000, in play, and would probably trigger more selling from miners whose costs sit well above the price. For Strategy shareholders, forced selling by index funds around the November 30 MSCI removal could widen the discount further before any rebound. Heavy options positioning could make moves in either direction more violent. A recovery in the ratio back above 1, as happened in July, would be the clearest sign that sellers are finished.

---

data.title: Five questions over Nvidia's China chip trail that Huang's return has not settled
data.description:
For Nvidia shareholders, the main risk is regulatory rather than personal. Tougher know-your-customer enforcement, or a revival of the push to require location tracking on chips, could slow shipments into Southeast Asia, which has been one of the company's biggest billing hubs. The stock already lost a large amount of market value during (well, prior to) the leadership crisis, so any new enforcement action or congressional hearing could hit sentiment quickly. Server makers such as Super Micro Computer are also exposed because of the pending prosecution. More broadly, the case adds to US-China tech tensions at a time when Washington's chip export policy is already in flux.

---

data.title: NZ consumer confidence breaks 100 as falling fuel prices cool inflation fears
data.description:
Households' inflation expectations have fallen sharply from their April peak, which eases one worry for the Reserve Bank of New Zealand. That leans slightly against any hawkish shift in the policy outlook and is a mild negative for the New Zealand dollar at the margin. The survey's market impact is usually small, though, and moves in global risk appetite and the US dollar are likely to matter more for the currency. The main sensitivity to watch is oil: these readings now follow pump prices closely, so a renewed jump in crude would probably undo much of this month's improvement.

---

data.title: Tokyo CPI preview: core inflation seen jumping to 3% three weeks before BoJ decision
data.description:
A firm Tokyo print would add support for the yen, which is still trading near 160 per dollar despite close to $100 billion of intervention. The Fed is also hiking, so the rate gap stays wide, and a BoJ hike on its own may not change the yen's direction much without signs of a quicker pace afterwards. Short-dated Japanese government bond yields are the most exposed if the core-core measure meets or beats forecast. A miss would likely weigh on the yen and could revive talk of the BoJ pausing, especially if Nikkei weakness continues.

---

data.title: EU leaders set to confirm backing for Spain's De Cos as next ECB President - report
data.description:
Reuters reports, citing EU diplomats, that EU leaders are set to sign off on Pablo Hernández de Cos as the next president of the European Central Bank.

This has been well telegraphed. Christine Lagarde is leaving early. She steps down on February 7, nine months before her eight-year term was due to end in October 2027. The timing is political. Leaving early lets EU leaders lock in a successor before April's French presidential election, where polls favour Marine Le Pen (and will be a major event in FX markets next year).

data.title: Connecting the dots: Is big tech starting to outgrow its own valuation playbook?
data.description:
One of the things that Wall Street has always loved about big tech is its ability to make an obscene amount of money without having to spend an equally obscene amount of money to grow. Or at least that used to be how it used to be.

Historically, the appeal of software and digital platforms has always been their ability to scale. Selling another million software subscriptions doesn't necessarily require building another factory. As such, revenues can grow much faster than the cost of doing business. And that is part of the reason Wall Street has been so comfortable attaching lofty valuations to tech stocks. However, the AI trade is a completely different beast.

data.title: What really drives the FX market? A look at interest rate differentials
data.description:
The FX market is highly sensitive to interest rates. This is one of the most important concepts to understand when trading currencies. In fact, interest rate differentials are the main drivers of major currencies.

 
The reason for this relationship is pretty simple: higher interest rates tend to attract foreign investment, increasing the demand and value of the currency. On the other hand, lower interest rates tend to be less attractive for foreign investment and decrease the currency's value. Therefore, monetary policy divergence (or better yet divergence in interest rate expectations) between two countries is the key driver.

data.title: Zcash continues to face macro headwinds despite improving adoption developments. What's next?
data.description:
Zcash continues to face a challenging macro environment, much like the broader crypto market, as tightening financial conditions, hawkish Fed and risk-off flows continue to weigh on risk appetite. Keep in mind that higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions are a headwind for risk assets, especially cryptocurrencies, which are sensitive to changes in liquidity and risk appetite.

Looking at Zcash-specific news, we have the ongoing governance debate over Zcash's development funding. Coinholders are voting until November 30 on a proposal to remove 50,000 ZEC (roughly $50 million at the time of the proposal) from the Community Grants treasury and redirect future funding towards a development and legal-defence fund. The proposal could improve the network's long-term funding structure, but it also introduces uncertainty around how development will be financed.
